title: Jollof Fried Chicken
author: Zoe Adjei
desc: Buttermilk-marinated strips in a cornflour and nutmeg coating, fried no more than three to four minutes — and the bread-cube oil test.
longDesc: A declared invention that works: jollof spice mix and buttermilk on chicken strips, a cornflour coating with nutmeg, and a short hot fry. Two tablespoons of the dry spice mix with salt, black pepper and a tablespoon of rapeseed oil go onto four chicken breasts cut into strips, with two hundred and fifty millilitres of buttermilk, and marinate at least one to two hours, preferably overnight. The oil goes to 180 to 190 degrees, or until a cube of bread browns in thirty seconds, and the strips fry no more than three to four minutes — succulent and juicy yet cooked through, golden and crispy but not burnt.
ingredients: 4 boneless, skinless chicken breasts, cut into strips
500 ml-1 litre vegetable oil, for deep frying
equipment: Thermometer, or a cube of bread
steps: Mix the jollof dry spice mix, salt, black pepper and rapeseed oil.
Coat the chicken strips, then add the buttermilk.
Marinate at least 1 to 2 hours, preferably overnight.
Combine the cornflour, black pepper, salt and nutmeg in a shallow dish.
Heat the oil to 180 to 190 degrees, or until a cube of bread browns in 30 seconds.
Dip each chicken strip into the seasoned cornflour — try to do 4 or 5 pieces in quick succession, as you need to drop them into the hot oil straight away.
Fry in batches for no more than 3 to 4 minutes, to keep them succulent and juicy yet cooked through, and golden and crispy but not burnt.
Drain on kitchen paper and keep hot.
chefTips: The bread-cube test is the best oil-temperature cue in this collection: a cube of bread should brown in thirty seconds. That is 180 to 190 degrees without a thermometer.
Four or five pieces coated in quick succession, then straight into the oil. Her instruction, and the reason is that cornflour on a wet marinade goes pasty if it sits.
Three to four minutes maximum. Strips, not pieces — they cook through fast and dry out faster.
Cornflour rather than wheat flour gives the shatter-crisp coating. It also makes the dish gluten-free if your spice mix is.
A teaspoon of nutmeg in the coating is what makes this taste Ghanaian rather than generic fried chicken.
Overnight beats the one-to-two-hour minimum. Buttermilk tenderises slowly.
It is a declared invention, not a traditional dish — fried chicken with a West African spice system. Enjoy it as that.
commonMistakes: Letting coated strips sit before frying.
Using wheat flour instead of cornflour.
Oil below temperature, which gives a soggy coating.
sources: Adapted from 'Jollof Fried Chicken' by Zoe Adjonyoh, from Zoe's Ghana Kitchen, published in two outlets WHOSE QUANTITIES AGREE: stylist.co.uk, 5 February 2021, byline 'By Stylist Team'; and dailymaverick.co.za, 31 March 2021, byline 'By The Reading List'. Confirmed across two fetches on both pages (TWO-PASS). Yield as printed: 'Serves 4'.

Ingredients exactly as printed: 2 tbsp jollof dry spice mix; ½ tsp sea salt; ½ tsp coarsely ground black pepper; 1 tbsp rapeseed oil; 4 boneless, skinless chicken breasts, cut into strips; 250ml buttermilk; 500ml–1 litre vegetable oil, for deep-frying. Coating: 150–200g cornflour; ½ tsp coarsely ground black pepper; ½ tsp sea salt; 1 tsp ground nutmeg.

Method and cues, verbatim from the Daily Maverick printing: marinate 'at least 1–2 hours, preferably overnight'; heat the oil 'to 180–190°C or until a cube of bread browns in 30 seconds'; 'Fry the chicken, in batches, for no more than 3–4 minutes to keep them succulent and juicy yet cooked through, and golden and crispy but not burnt.'; 'Dip each chicken strip into the seasoned cornflour... try to do 4 or 5 pieces in quick succession, as you need to drop them into the hot oil straight away.' The Stylist printing adds: drain on kitchen paper and keep hot.
THE BREAD-CUBE TEST is the most practical oil-temperature cue in this whole collection and is reproduced verbatim.

A DECLARED INVENTION: fried chicken is not a traditional Ghanaian dish, and this is her West African spice system applied to an American form. It is published as a diaspora invention rather than as traditional cooking, and the community field says so.
IT DEPENDS ON the jollof dry spice mix at GHA101, whose two printings differ substantially — so which version you made will change this dish.

THE BOTH-OUTLETS AGREEMENT is worth noting: unlike her spice mix, her chalé sauce and her peanut sauce — each of which has printings that disagree — this recipe is identical across two publications, which makes its quantities the most secure of her repertoire in this collection.

ON THE GLUTEN STATUS: cornflour rather than wheat flour makes the coating gluten-free, but the dish is not tagged gluten-free here because the optional prawn powder and the spice mix's provenance are not guaranteed.
storage: Best at once. 2 days refrigerated, though the coating softens.
reheating: A hot oven to re-crisp. Never the microwave.
healthBenefits: Chicken breast is very lean and high in protein.
Nutmeg and the spice mix contribute antioxidant compounds.
A short fry absorbs less oil than a long one.
culturalNote: Fried chicken with a Ghanaian spice system is exactly the kind of thing diaspora cooking produces, and the bread-cube oil test is a reminder that useful technique travels regardless of which cuisine it starts in. That this is the one recipe of hers whose two printings agree perfectly is a small pleasure in a collection full of contradictions.
